video_title: Why Private Credit Got Entangled With Insurance | Odd Lots
gist: Law professor Andrew Granato and Yale financial economist Pranjal Drall argue that the deep tie-up between private equity/private credit and US life insurers is driven less by asset-liability synergy than by an implicit, socialized backstop: state insurance guaranty funds are post-funded, assessed on premium volume rather than risk, and offset by tax credits in ~44 states, making them a stealth taxpayer bailout that subsidizes aggressive investing. They pair that with the opacity of private-letter-rated private credit on insurer balance sheets, Bermuda 'shadow reinsurance', and the fact that no large national life insurer failure has ever been run through the guaranty-fund system.

themes.theme: Why PE bought the insurance balance sheet

insights.claim: The PE-insurance 'flywheel' is a three-subsidiary structure — a buyout arm, a private credit fund, and a life insurer — where the insurer's long-dated liabilities warehouse the illiquid loans the credit arm originates to the buyout arm's portfolio companies.
insights.speaker: guest (paper co-author)
insights.so_what: Understanding the loop tells you where losses would actually surface: not in the PE fund, but on the regulated insurer's balance sheet.
insights.quote: McKinsey has called this a flywheel. So imagine you have like a private equity firm with three subsidiaries.

insights.claim: Roughly $750 billion of US life insurance assets now sit within private equity's purview, and PE-owned insurers are shifting portfolios away from the traditional stodgy triple-A corporate bond book toward affiliated private credit.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Sizes the channel: a $750bn pool whose asset mix is migrating from public IG bonds to illiquid, thinly-marked loans.

insights.claim: Warren Buffett pioneered the same core insight decades ago — that an insurance arm is an extraordinary source of patient capital that lets an investor hold through drawdowns — so the PE-insurance pairing is not new; what changed in the last 15 years is the aggression of the investment strategy layered on top, since a life insurer's permanent capital frees the manager from LPs constantly demanding returns.
insights.speaker: guest (paper co-author)
insights.so_what: Separates the legitimate float thesis from the new risk: the structure is old, the asset quality and affiliation are what's new.

insights.claim: PE-affiliated insurer arrangements sit on a spectrum from a competitive third-party mandate to the problematic case where the insurer's balance sheet is effectively controlled by a bigger asset manager and has little investment discretion.
insights.speaker: Pranjal Drall (guest, Yale JD/PhD candidate in financial economics)
insights.so_what: A screening test for insurer credits: who negotiates the mandate determines whether fees and asset selection are arm's length.
insights.quote: the insurer balance sheet is effectively in control of a bigger asset manager

insights.claim: PE-sponsored insurers pay fees not just for asset management but for a stack of affiliated services — accounting, valuation consulting and more — so the insurer's balance sheet is a holding pattern for assets while the economics accrue outside the insurer's corporate form.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Fee leakage to affiliates is where policyholder returns quietly go; look for related-party service fees, not just the management fee.
insights.quote: the balance sheet of the insurer is a holding pattern for a lot of the assets

themes.theme: Guaranty funds vs the FDIC: a worse backstop

insights.claim: Unlike the FDIC's pre-funded, risk-based deposit insurance fund, state insurance guaranty funds levy assessments on surviving insurers only after an insolvency has already happened — meaning the failed insurer itself contributes $0 toward its own resolution.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Post-funding removes any ex-ante cost of risk-taking, the single biggest structural difference from banking.
insights.quote: But this assessment is only levied after the insolvency has already happened.

insights.claim: In about 34 states insurers get a full tax credit against guaranty-fund assessments taken 20% a year over five years, in another ten states over roughly ten years, and only about six states give no credit at all — making the backstop economically equivalent to a taxpayer bailout that no legislature ever votes on.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: The 'private' insurance backstop is fiscally public in ~44 states — a hidden contingent liability for state budgets and a subsidy to insurer risk.
insights.quote: if you have a fully offsetting tax credit, this is economically equivalent to a taxpayer bailout of the insurance policyholders.

insights.claim: The guaranty-fund cap of roughly $200-300K per policy covers only about the 40th percentile of life insurance policies, so coverage is materially worse than the FDIC's $250K deposit cap given that life policyholders skew wealthy.
insights.speaker: Pranjal Drall (guest, Yale JD/PhD candidate in financial economics)
insights.so_what: The system has the taxpayer cost of a bailout without the confidence benefit — a majority of policy value is uninsured.
insights.quote: close to 200 K for life insurance. That's about the 40th percentile of life insurer policies. A lot of policies are way bigger than that.

insights.claim: The guaranty-fund system has never been tested by the insolvency of a large national life insurer with hundreds of billions of dollars of assets — AIG in 2008 was bailed out rather than resolved — and any such failure would require simultaneous state-court proceedings in every state at once, with no federal insurance regulator.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Untested plumbing plus a much larger and riskier asset base is the tail risk to underwrite in insurer credit and annuity counterparty exposure.
insights.quote: Iowa and Oregon and New York and Tennessee sort of doing this at the same time is a very challenging task. We haven't really had major insurer failure in this way.

insights.claim: In states without tax credits, post-insolvency assessments create a perverse feedback loop: a bad macro environment knocks over a large insurer, survivors are billed at the worst possible moment, and that can push additional insurers into insolvency — with spiking interest rates worsening the time-value cost of credits spread over 5-10 years.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Identifies a pro-cyclical contagion channel unique to insurance — assessments hit exactly when survivors are weakest.
insights.quote: that levy is assessments on other insurers that are already hurting.

themes.theme: Moral hazard baked into the design

insights.claim: Because assessments are only paid post-insolvency, a rational insurer heading into distress is incentivized to take on more risk and to offer unusually generous policy terms to win premiums today, since it will never pay for the resulting failure.
insights.speaker: Pranjal Drall (guest, Yale JD/PhD candidate in financial economics)
insights.so_what: Anomalously attractive annuity/policy pricing from a stressed insurer is a warning signal, not a bargain.
insights.quote: One more thing that might the regime encourages is as you head into distress, you want to take on more risk.

insights.claim: Unlike banking — where FDIC rules cap the deposit rates a troubled bank can offer — insurance has no equivalent mechanism to stop a desperate insurer from bidding aggressively for new business.
insights.speaker: Pranjal Drall (guest, Yale JD/PhD candidate in financial economics)
insights.so_what: A missing circuit-breaker: zombie insurers can grow their book right up to failure, enlarging the eventual assessment.

insights.claim: Guaranty-fund assessments are weighted purely by premium volume rather than risk-weighted like bank assessments, so two insurers with identical premiums — one conservative, one investing 'like a madman' — get the same bill while the risky one extracts a far larger expected public subsidy.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: The backstop is an implicit cross-subsidy from conservative insurers to aggressive ones — a structural tailwind for the most aggressive balance sheets until it breaks.
insights.quote: But for guarantee funds it's purely the premium volume.

insights.claim: Running private credit through a life insurer rather than a private credit fund means the creditor base is a dispersed retail policyholder pool, a large fraction of whom are fully guaranteed and therefore have no reason to monitor — so the level of examination the manager faces is far lower.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Explains why the insurer wrapper is preferred for the riskiest assets: monitoring, not just duration, is the arbitrage.
insights.quote: the level of kind of examination that you're going to get from your creditors is so much lower.

themes.theme: Valuation opacity and private letter ratings

insights.claim: State insurance regulators see only the value reported to them for private credit holdings — typically outsourced to a third-party rating agency and translated into a 1-to-10 capital notch — so regulatory capital rests entirely on ratings the regulator does not independently verify.
insights.speaker: Pranjal Drall (guest, Yale JD/PhD candidate in financial economics)
insights.so_what: Insurer capital ratios are only as good as private-letter ratings; the reported RBC cushion may be largely fictional.
insights.quote: And all the insurer regulator sees is the value reported to them

insights.claim: Private letter ratings used by life insurers are not publicly visible, so no outsider can investigate how a rating was obtained or compare it against a track record — reproducing the 2008 credit-rating incentive problem in a less observable venue.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: The ratings-arbitrage channel is invisible to public-market analysts; disclosure changes here would be the catalyst that repricess insurer credit.
insights.quote: These are ratings where, the rating itself is actually not kind of publicly visible.

insights.claim: Ratings inflation penalizes good insurance asset managers in equilibrium: a manager holding genuinely investment-grade private credit gets the same rating as one holding a middle-market loan, so high-quality private credit loses its competitive advantage rather than merely hiding risk.
insights.speaker: Pranjal Drall (guest, Yale JD/PhD candidate in financial economics)
insights.so_what: Second-order effect: opacity drives adverse selection toward worse assets industry-wide, not just at the bad actors.
insights.quote: it's sort of hard to tell what's like a truly good private credit loan versus not.

insights.claim: The annuity puzzle — that annuities are theoretically the perfect product yet society under-buys them because prices are too high and policies aren't good — suggests the end market has never been effectively competitive, though some empirical data shows PE-owned insurers compete better on terms because they earn money elsewhere in the flywheel.
insights.speaker: Pranjal Drall (guest, Yale JD/PhD candidate in financial economics)
insights.so_what: Consumers may genuinely get better headline annuity pricing from PE-owned insurers — the cost shows up decades later as credit risk.
insights.quote: in some ways a shop that owns an insurer might offer better terms to policyholders because they have all these other ways to make money, from the business.

insights.claim: Insurers hold roughly 10-15% of assets in private credit, and if a third of private credit is software lending, a large slice of that exposure could sit in a single industry — a concentration regulators are far less equipped to police than bank examiners policing loan books.
insights.speaker: Pranjal Drall (guest, Yale JD/PhD candidate in financial economics)
insights.so_what: Frames the concrete correlated-loss scenario for insurers: a software/SaaS credit cycle transmitted through affiliated private credit.
insights.quote: insurers or something like 15% of the assets are in private credit, 10 to 15, depending how you measure.

insights.claim: Whole life policies with cash value reserve accounts carry rights of withdrawal, making them functionally demand deposits — so an insurer that sold a lot of cash-value policies can in fact be run on, undercutting the blanket assumption that insurers are run-proof.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Screen insurer liability mixes for cash-value and surrenderable products, not just annuity duration, when assessing run risk.
insights.quote: you have rights of withdrawal on that account. And you and so that that is a demand deposit like.

insights.claim: Runs on life insurers have happened before — Executive Life in the early 1990s was run on while struggling — but at only a few billion dollars of assets it was too small to threaten the system, so the sector's run-proof reputation is partly luck.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Historical precedent exists for insurer runs; the untested variable is scale, not mechanism.
insights.quote: So executive life in the early 1990s was a life insurer that was really struggling. And there was a run on on the insurer.

insights.claim: 'Shadow reinsurance' — ceding assets and liabilities to captive reinsurers in Bermuda or in states like Iowa and Vermont that compete with it — offers low tax rates and, critically, eliminates balance-sheet visibility that regulators otherwise have at high quality on a quarterly, CUSIP-level basis.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Reported insurer holdings understate exposure; the ceded book in Bermuda captives is where the real risk concentration can hide.
insights.quote: once the that is reentered into one of these quote unquote shadow reinsurers, you lose all visibility into what's going on.

insights.claim: State-only insurance regulation persists because an 1800s Supreme Court case held insurance was not interstate commerce, and when the Court reversed in the 1940s Congress immediately disclaimed the power via McCarran-Ferguson, reserving all authority to states absent explicit federal legislation.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Federal reform requires an affirmative act of Congress — the default is inertia, so don't expect regulatory fixes without a failure first.
insights.quote: says that you know, unless Congress explicitly passes a law that says we're regulating insurers, all other regulatory authority is reserved to the states.

insights.claim: The national association of state insurance regulators is a DC nonprofit that is not formally a public entity and funds itself by selling data to insurers, while some states — Indiana among them — automatically incorporate its model laws including prospective future changes into their own state law.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: The de facto rule-writer for US insurance is a privately funded body whose customers are the regulated — a governance weak point in any reform scenario.
insights.quote: I think Indiana is one of these states where they self incorporate the model law, that the NRC puts out even prospective changes.

insights.claim: The proposed fix ladder is: a Pigouvian-style capital surcharge on opacity itself for assets that are structurally hard to value, ending the tax credits on guaranty-fund assessments, moving guaranty funds to pre-funding on an FDIC model, and importing banking's source-of-strength doctrine so affiliates of a failed insurer must fund the payouts.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: A surcharge-on-opacity regime would hit PE-affiliated insurers hardest and is the specific policy risk to watch for insurance-linked PE valuations.
insights.quote: you can do a Peruvian tax on opacity itself where you say like, oh, if certain kinds of assets are just structurally hard to value

insights.claim: Applying a source-of-strength doctrine to insurance groups would let regulators require other affiliates in any insurance holding group — PE-sponsored or not — to fund a set percentage of guaranty-fund payouts, aligning downside risk with the parties actually controlling the investments.
insights.speaker: Andrew Granato (guest, UT Austin law professor)
insights.so_what: Would convert an off-balance-sheet subsidy into a real contingent liability for PE sponsors — a direct valuation hit if ever adopted.
insights.quote: So you could go to the other affiliates in any insurance group, whether it's private equity or not

themes.theme: Live case: Guggenheim, Delaware Life and affiliated assets

insights.claim: Federal prosecutors are reportedly investigating Mark Walter — LA Dodgers owner and principal behind Guggenheim, which has affiliated insurers Delaware Life and Clear Spring — over the insurers' affiliated-asset disclosures.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal (host)
insights.so_what: The first enforcement-driven test of affiliated-asset disclosure at a PE-linked insurer — a template for how this risk surfaces publicly.

insights.claim: Under investigation, the Guggenheim-affiliated insurers issued a revised disclosure restating affiliated assets from roughly 3-5% of total assets to about 40% — a twelvefold revision that illustrates how little outsiders know about related-party exposure on insurer balance sheets.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal (host)
insights.so_what: Treat reported affiliated-asset percentages at PE-linked insurers as a floor, not an estimate; restatements of this size can move an entire credit.
insights.quote: It moved from 3 to 40%. So these are the kind of concerns that I think are starting to bubble up.

insights.claim: Policymakers deliberately pushed credit risk out of the regulated banking system into private credit vehicles so losses would be borne by investors rather than socialized — but that risk is now migrating back into insurance, another regulated industry with its own public backstop, defeating the original purpose.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway (host)
insights.so_what: The core macro-prudential argument: the post-GFC risk transfer may have been a round trip, with the destination less well supervised than the origin.

insights.claim: Banks and insurers are fundamentally the same business with a different redemption schedule — the distinction is only the timing and liquidity with which claimants can get money out — which is why insurance policyholders, like depositors, are the category society refuses to let bear losses.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal (host)
insights.so_what: If policyholders are politically protected like depositors, insurer risk-taking carries an implicit public put — price insurer-linked equity accordingly.
insights.quote: it's kind of the same, different, the same business with a different sort of redemption schedule.
